In an r-graph, every H⊆G with |V(H)|=2k+1 has at least r edges leaving, so |E(H)| ≤ rk, and |V(H)|=2k gives |E(H)| ≤ rk; hence the overfull parameter w(G) ≤ r. Goldberg then gives χ' ≤ max{Δ+1, w} = r+1, which is Seymour's r-graph conjecture.

For an r-graph G, Δ(G)=r, and for any H⊆G with |V(H)| odd the cut condition gives |E(H)| ≤ (r|V(H)|−r)/2, so ⌈|E(H)|/⌊|V(H)|/2⌋⌉ ≤ r; for even |V(H)| the ratio is ≤ r by regularity. Hence w(G) ≤ r+1 and Goldberg's bound χ' ≤ max{Δ+1, w} yields χ' ≤ r+1.

For an r-graph, Delta = r and every H on an odd vertex set S has |E(H)| <= (r|S|-r)/2 since at least r edges leave S, so the overfull parameter w(G) <= r. Goldberg's bound chi' <= max(Delta+1, w) then gives chi' <= r+1, which is Seymour's r-graph conjecture (the classical Goldberg-Seymour link).
χ''(G) ≤ χ''_ℓ(G) always; so χ''_ℓ ≤ Δ+2 for all simple graphs gives χ'' ≤ Δ+2, i.e. the Total Colouring Conjecture.
χ''(G) ≤ χ''_ℓ(G) always, so χ''_ℓ(G) ≤ Δ+2 for every simple graph gives χ''(G) ≤ Δ+2, which is the Total Colouring Conjecture (the paper itself presents it as the list analogue of TCC).
Part (a) says χ_f(G) ≤ had(G). If G is K_{t+1}-minor-free then had(G) ≤ t, so χ_f(G) ≤ t; since α(G)·χ_f(G) ≥ n, we get α(G) ≥ n/t.

If G has no K_{t+1} minor then had(G) <= t, so part (a) chi_f(G) <= had(G) gives chi_f(G) <= t; fractional colouring always yields alpha(G) >= n/chi_f(G) >= n/t, which is the conjectured independence-number bound.

Part (a) of Fractional Hadwiger says χ_f(G) ≤ had(G). If G is K_{t+1}-minor-free then had(G) ≤ t, so χ_f(G) ≤ t; since χ_f(G) ≥ n/α(G) always, α(G) ≥ n/t, which is exactly the independence-number conjecture.
χ(G) ≤ χ_ℓ(G), so the list version χ_ℓ ≤ ⌈(Δ+1+ω)/2⌉ immediately implies Reed's conjecture for the chromatic number.
χ(G) ≤ χ_ℓ(G) for every graph, so the list-chromatic version χ_ℓ(G) ≤ ⌈(Δ+1+ω)/2⌉ immediately yields Reed's conjecture χ(G) ≤ ⌈(Δ+1+ω)/2⌉.

For triangle-free G, ω ≤ 2 and Reed's bound gives χ ≤ ⌈(Δ+3)/2⌉, which equals ⌈Δ/2⌉+2 for even Δ and ⌈Δ/2⌉+1 for odd Δ; hence Reed's conjecture implies χ ≤ ⌈Δ/2⌉+2 for triangle-free graphs, exactly the ω≤2 instance.

Both are the polynomial strengthening of Gyárfás–Sumner: for every forest H, the class of H-free graphs is polynomially χ-bounded.

Both state the polynomial Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture verbatim: for every forest H there is a polynomial f with χ(G) ≤ f(ω(G)) for every H-free graph G ('every forest is good').
Both state that the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture holds with a χ-bounding function polynomial in the clique number, i.e. polynomial χ-boundedness of T-free classes for every forest/tree T.
Polynomial χ-boundedness of H-free graphs for every forest H in particular provides some χ-bounding function for every tree T, which is exactly the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture.

A polynomial χ-bounding function is in particular a χ-bounding function, and every tree is a forest, so polynomial χ-boundedness of H-free classes for all forests H implies the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture.

The 'if' direction for oriented forests implies Gyárfás–Sumner: given a tree T, fix any orientation H; an undirected T-free graph G, arbitrarily oriented, contains no induced copy of H, so χ-boundedness of Forb(H) bounds χ(G) by f(ω). Aboulker et al. state this generalization explicitly.
Oriented stars are oriented forests, so χ-boundedness of Forb(S) for every oriented star S is the restriction of the 'if' direction of the general forest conjecture to stars.
P_t is a forest, so η-boundedness of P_t-free graphs (t≥6) is the restriction of the η-boundedness conjecture for all forests H to H=P_t.
Paths P_t are forests, so the η-boundedness conjecture for P_t-free graphs (t ≥ 6) is Conjecture 1.8 restricted to H = P_t; the paper notes the cases t ≤ 5 are already proved.
P_t is a forest, so the conjecture that H-free graphs are eta-bounded for every forest H specializes to the class of P_t-free graphs (t>=6).
A disjoint union of two stars S_a∪S_b is a forest; the record itself asks whether this family satisfies the general forest conjecture (their Conjecture 1.8), so it is the H=S_a∪S_b instance.
The disjoint union of two stars S_a ∪ S_b is a forest; the record explicitly poses this as the instance of Conjecture 1.8 (η-boundedness of H-free graphs for every forest H) with H = S_a ∪ S_b.

The disjoint union of two stars S_a cup S_b is a forest, so eta-boundedness of (S_a cup S_b)-free graphs is the instance H = S_a cup S_b of the forest conjecture (the paper poses it as the open case of its Conjecture 1.8).

Both assert: for all k (clique bound) and ℓ, graphs with ω<k and sufficiently large χ contain holes of ℓ consecutive lengths; the formulations 'contains K_κ or ℓ consecutive holes' and 'ω<k and χ≥n forces ν consecutive holes' are the same statement.

Planar duality: G planar with girth ≥ 4k iff its dual G* is 4k-edge-connected, and a modular (2k+1)-orientation of G* is equivalent (Tutte flow/coloring duality) to a circular (2+1/k)-coloring of G, i.e. a homomorphism to C_{2k+1}. So the mapping conjecture is Jaeger's conjecture restricted to duals of planar graphs.

Restrict Jaeger's conjecture to planar graphs and dualize: girth ≥ 4k of G means the planar dual G* is 4k-edge-connected; a modular (2k+1)-orientation of G* is a (2+1/k)-flow, which dualizes to a (2+1/k)-coloring of G, i.e. a homomorphism to C_{2k+1}. The OPG entry states this duality explicitly.

This is Jaeger's modular orientation conjecture restricted to planar graphs and dualized: for planar dual pairs, girth(G) = edge-connectivity(G*), a modular (2k+1)-orientation of G* is a (2+1/k)-flow, and a (2+1/k)-flow of G* corresponds to a (2+1/k)-circular-coloring of G, i.e. a homomorphism G -> C_{2k+1}. The OPG page states this duality explicitly.
Tournaments are digraphs, so majority 3-colourability of every tournament is the restriction of the majority 3-colouring conjecture for all digraphs.
Majority 3-colourability of tournaments is the restriction of the majority 3-colouring conjecture for all digraphs to the subclass of tournaments.

Tournaments are digraphs, so the conjecture that every digraph has a majority 3-colouring immediately yields a majority 3-colouring of every tournament; the tournament question is the restriction of Conjecture (every digraph) to the class of tournaments.
Tournaments are digraphs, so 'every digraph has a majority 3-colouring' restricted to tournaments is exactly the source question.
Eulerian digraphs are digraphs, so majority 3-colourability of Eulerian digraphs is a restriction of the conjecture that every digraph has a majority 3-colouring.
Majority 3-colourability of Eulerian digraphs is the restriction of the majority 3-colouring conjecture for all digraphs to the subclass of Eulerian digraphs.
Eulerian digraphs are digraphs, so the majority 3-colouring conjecture for all digraphs restricted to the class of Eulerian digraphs is exactly this problem.
Eulerian digraphs are a subclass of all digraphs, so the conjecture that every digraph has a majority 3-colouring immediately yields the Eulerian case.
Eulerian digraphs are digraphs, so the majority-3-colouring conjecture for all digraphs restricted to Eulerian digraphs is exactly the source question.

The k=2 case of the 1/k-conjecture is a 3-colouring in which each vertex has at most half of its out-neighbours in its own colour, which is exactly a majority 3-colouring. (The general 1/k statement was disproved for some k, but the k=2 instance is the majority 3-colouring conjecture.)

Setting k=2 in the generalized conjecture ((k+1)-colouring with at most (1/k)deg⁺(v) same-coloured out-neighbours) gives exactly a majority 3-colouring (3 colours, at most half of out-neighbours same-coloured).

The k=2 instance of 'every digraph has a (k+1)-colouring with at most deg+(v)/k same-coloured out-neighbours' is precisely a majority 3-colouring; the paper states Conjecture 9 as the natural generalisation of Conjecture 2.

Burr's conjecture gives: every digraph with chromatic number ≥ 2k-2 contains every oriented tree T of order k as a subdigraph; a copy of T is in particular a subdivision of T, so mader_χ(T) ≤ 2k-2. (Both statements use the chromatic number of the underlying graph.)

If every digraph with χ ≥ 2k−2 contains every oriented tree T of order k as a subdigraph (Burr's conjecture), then in particular it contains T itself, which is a subdivision of T, so mader_χ(T) ≤ 2k−2; the paper states Conjecture __03 is a direct consequence of Burr's conjecture.

Burr's conjecture: (dichromatic/chromatic) number >= 2k-2 forces every oriented tree of order k as a subdigraph. A copy of T is itself a (trivial) subdivision of T, hence mader_chi(T) <= 2k-2. Since chi >= dichromatic chi-vec, the implication holds under either reading of the colouring parameter.

Burr's conjecture: every digraph with chromatic number >= 2k-2 contains every oriented tree T of order k as a subdigraph. Since T is a subdivision of itself (and chi >= dichromatic number, covering either reading of the mader parameter), any such digraph contains a subdivision of T, so mader_chi(T) <= 2k-2.

Burr's conjecture gives every oriented tree T of order k as a subdigraph of any digraph with chi >= 2k-2; T is a trivial subdivision of itself, so mader_chi(T) <= 2k-2. The paper states this as a direct consequence of Burr's conjecture.

A graph contains a cycle iff its degeneracy is ≥ 2, so 'some out-neighbourhood contains a cycle' is exactly the d=2 instance of 'some out-neighbourhood has degeneracy ≥ d' for graphs of sufficiently large chromatic number.

A graph contains a cycle iff it has degeneracy ≥ 2, so the cycle-in-out-neighbourhood conjecture is exactly the d=2 case of the question whether high χ forces an out-neighbourhood of degeneracy ≥ d (the paper says it is the case d=2 of Question 10).

A graph contains a cycle iff it has degeneracy >= 2, so the cycle-in-out-neighbourhood conjecture is exactly the d=2 case of the degeneracy question; the paper explicitly presents Conjecture 11 as the case d=2 of Question 10.

The d=2 instance: a graph of degeneracy >= 2 contains a subgraph of minimum degree 2 and hence a cycle (graphs of degeneracy <= 1 are exactly forests). So forcing out-neighbourhood degeneracy >= 2 at some vertex forces a cycle in G[N+_T(v)].
A graph has degeneracy >= 2 iff it contains a cycle, so the cycle-in-out-neighbourhood statement is exactly the d=2 instance of the degeneracy question; the authors present it as such.

Both ask whether 4-colorability of graphs embedded in a fixed surface can be tested in polynomial time; the sphere case is trivial by the Four Color Theorem, so 'fixed surface' and 'fixed surface other than the sphere' state the same open problem.

Both ask the complexity of 3-colourability on P_t-free graphs for large t: 1803.05396__00 asks to determine it for t >= 8 (smaller t known polynomial), 1806.11196__00 conjectures polynomial for every fixed t; the open content is identical.

P_t is a graph all of whose components are paths, so 'if every component of H is a path then 3-Coloring on H-free graphs is polytime' yields, for H=P_t, a polynomial-time 3-coloring algorithm on P_t-free graphs for every t.
A single path P_t is a linear forest (every component a path), so polynomial 3-Coloring on H-free graphs for all path-component H restricted to H = P_t gives exactly the P_t-free 3-coloring question.
The k-Coloring dichotomy problem for H-free graphs (all k≥3, all H) contains as the k=3, H=P_t instance the question of the complexity of 3-colourability of P_t-free graphs.

A graph is 5-choosable iff it contains no subgraph critical for 5-choosability, and 5-colorable iff it contains no 6-critical subgraph. If on the torus these two families of critical graphs coincide, then a toroidal graph is 5-choosable iff it is 5-colorable.

A toroidal graph is not 5-choosable iff it contains a subgraph critical for 5-choosability, and not 5-colorable iff it contains a 6-critical subgraph. If the two families of critical graphs coincide on the torus, the two failure conditions coincide, so 5-choosable iff 5-colorable.

If every forest is good (H-free class polynomially χ-bounded), then in particular the disjoint union of any two good trees, being a forest, is good.

A majority 3-colouring is a 3-colouring with at most (1/2)deg+(v) same-coloured out-neighbours, so beta=1/2 < 1 answers the sublinear question affirmatively.

The paper states the odd-k case of determining R_ℓ(K_{1,2},k) is equivalent to the List Colouring Conjecture for cliques of even order (whether χ'_ℓ(K_n)=χ'(K_n)=n−1 for even n); the full LCC for multigraphs thus settles it as its restriction to even complete graphs.

Both concern the same quantity — the supremum/infimum behaviour of fractional chromatic numbers of planar graphs with no C4 or C5 — one asking its value, the other whether the proven 11/3 bound is tight; a single determination problem stated twice.

Every induced copy of a tree T is in particular a path-induced copy, so graphs with no path-induced copy of (T,r) are T-free; polynomial Gyárfás–Sumner then bounds their chromatic number by a polynomial in ω(G) ≤ t, answering Question __00 affirmatively.

Part (a) of Fractional Hadwiger states chi_f(G) <= had(G). If alpha(G) <= 2 then chi_f(G) >= n/alpha(G) >= n/2, so had(G) >= n/2, and since had is an integer G has a K_{ceil(n/2)} minor, which is exactly the seagull statement.

Suppose alpha(G) <= 2 and G has no K_{ceil(n/2)} minor. Apply the target with t+1 = ceil(n/2): alpha(G) >= n/(ceil(n/2)-1) > 2 for every n (check n even: n/(n/2-1) > 2; n odd: 2n/(n-1) > 2), a contradiction. So the alpha >= n/t conjecture implies the seagull problem (its alpha = 2 case).

Contrapositive with t = ⌈n/2⌉−1: if G has no K_{⌈n/2⌉} minor, it is K_{t+1}-minor-free, so α(G) ≥ n/t ≥ n/((n−1)/2) > 2, i.e. α(G) ≥ 3. Hence α(G) ≤ 2 forces a K_{⌈n/2⌉} minor, which is the Seagull problem (the known α=2 case of the Hadwiger-weakening α ≥ n/t).

Let G have no independent set of size 3 (alpha <= 2) and let h be its Hadwiger number; G is K_{h+1}-minor-free, so the conjecture gives 2 >= alpha >= n/h, hence h >= n/2, i.e. G has a K_{ceil(n/2)} minor. The seagull problem is the alpha=2 case of the alpha >= n/t conjecture.

Digraphs with min semidegree >= f form a subclass of those with min out-degree >= f, so Mader's out-degree conjecture implies the semidegree version. Conversely the paper (arXiv:1610.00876) proves mader_{delta+}(TT_k) <= mader_{delta0}(TT_{2k}), so the semidegree version implies the out-degree version; the paper states the two conjectures are equivalent.

A non-null 6-regular graph has minimum degree exactly 6 and maximum degree 6 <= 8, so it satisfies the hypotheses of the statement 'min degree >= 6 and max degree <= 8 forces a K_6 minor'; the 6-regular conjecture is the regular special case.

A 6-regular graph has minimum degree 6 and maximum degree 6 ≤ 8, so the class of Conjecture 1.3 is contained in the class of the parenthetical strengthening (δ≥6, Δ≤8), with identical conclusion (K6 minor). The paper itself calls the latter 'a stronger open belief than Conjecture 1.3'.
A 6-regular graph has minimum degree 6 and maximum degree 6 <= 8, so the min-degree-6/max-degree-8 statement restricted to 6-regular graphs is Conjecture 1.3; the paper calls it a stronger belief.

Jorgensen implies the second half of the target (every 7-connected graph has a K_6 minor): a 7-connected graph with no K_6 minor would be apex, but deleting the apex vertex leaves a 6-connected planar graph, impossible since planar graphs are at most 5-connected. The first half (min degree 7) is not covered, so this is an implication to only one of the entry's two statements.

The n = 6 instance of the target says every sufficiently large 6-connected K_6-minor-free graph has 1 vertex whose deletion leaves a planar graph, i.e. is apex — exactly Jorgensen restricted to large graphs. The n=6 instance of Thomas's problem states every sufficiently large 6-connected K6-minor-free graph has 6−5=1 vertex whose deletion leaves a planar graph, i.e. is apex — Jørgensen's conjecture restricted to sufficiently large graphs. K_{t-1,t-1} has a K_t minor (contract t-2 disjoint edges of a perfect matching; the two leftover vertices from opposite sides are adjacent and complete to the contracted clique). Hence K_t-minor-free graphs are K_{t-1,t-1}-minor-free, and the target of Question 2 with s = t' = t-1 gives chi_l(G) <= 2(t-1)+(t-1) = 3t-3, i.e. List Hadwiger with c = 3.
The t = 3 instance of h(t) = ceil(3(t-1)/2) gives h(3) = 3, i.e. every K_3-minor-free hypergraph is 3-colorable, which is exactly the source problem.

Conjecture 2 asserts every K_t-minor-free hypergraph is ⌈3(t−1)/2⌉-colorable for all t≥2; setting t=3 gives ⌈3·2/2⌉=3, i.e. every K_3-minor-free hypergraph is 3-colorable, which is exactly Problem 1. The paper itself states Problem 1 isolates the smallest open case of Conjecture 2.
Setting t=3 in h(t)=ceil(3(t-1)/2) gives h(3)=3, i.e. every K_3-minor-free hypergraph is 3-colorable; the target conjecture thus contains the K_3 question as its t=3 instance.

If (even hole, diamond)-free graphs have tree-alpha <= a, take a tree decomposition witnessing it for an (even hole, K_4, diamond)-free graph: each bag has independence number <= a and clique number <= 3, so by Ramsey each bag has at most R(a+1,4) vertices, giving bounded treewidth — the target's question.

(even hole, K4, diamond)-free graphs are (even hole, diamond)-free, so bounded tree-α applies. In a tree-decomposition with bags of independence number ≤ a, K4-freeness bounds each bag by Ramsey R(a+1,4), giving bounded treewidth, hence a positive answer to the (even hole, K4, diamond)-free treewidth question.

(even hole, K_4, diamond)-free graphs form a subclass of (even hole, diamond)-free graphs with omega <= 3. If tree-independence number is bounded by t, each bag of the decomposition has independence <= t and clique < 4, hence size < R(4,t+1) by Ramsey, so treewidth is bounded (and bounded treewidth implies bounded cliquewidth).

Every C_4, theta, prism and even wheel contains an even hole (C_4 is one; for theta/prism, two of the three connecting paths share parity, giving an even hole; an even wheel has a sector cycle of even length). Same sign argument: for bridgeless G, Phi(G,6)>0 (Seymour), Phi positive at infinity, and no real root in (4,infinity) forces Phi(G,5)>0, i.e. G has a nowhere-zero Z_5-flow, equivalent to a nowhere-zero 5-flow.
For 2-edge-connected G the flow polynomial is monic (positive for large x) and nonzero; if it has no real root exceeding 4 it stays positive on (4,∞), in particular Φ(G,5.5)>0.
The flow polynomial is monic, so if every real root of Q_G is at most 4, then Q_G(t)>0 for all real t>4, and in particular Phi(G,5.5)>0 for every 2-edge-connected G.

For 2-edge-connected G, Phi(G,6)>0 by Seymour's 6-flow theorem, so Phi is a nonzero polynomial, positive for large x. If Phi has no real root >4, it cannot change sign on (4,infinity), hence Phi(G,5.5)>0.

A class-1 (2t+1)-regular graph decomposes into 2t+1 perfect matchings; every odd vertex set X meets each matching's cut ∂(X) at least once, so |∂(X)|≥2t+1, i.e., the graph is a (2t+1)-graph. Hence for t>1 the class-1 conjecture (F_c≤2+2/t) is the restriction of the r-graph conjecture; the remaining t=1 case is Tutte's theorem (3-edge-colorable cubic ⟹ F_c≤4). Both statements are now disproved, consistently with this containment.

A (2t+1)-regular class-1 graph decomposes into 2t+1 perfect matchings, each meeting every odd vertex cut, so every odd cut has size at least 2t+1, i.e. the graph is a (2t+1)-graph. Hence the r-graph conjecture F_c <= 2+2/t restricts to the class-1 conjecture; the OPG page states this containment (the leftover t=1 case of the source is a known theorem for cubic graphs).

Every (2t+1)-regular class-1 graph is a (2t+1)-graph: its 2t+1 disjoint perfect matchings each meet every odd cut, so odd cuts have size >= 2t+1. Hence the r-graph conjecture (F_c <= 2+2/t) restricted to class-1 regular graphs gives the class-1 conjecture (the t=1 case is classical via 3-edge-coloring => 4-flow). OPG states the containment explicitly.

The entry's two conjectures together imply the 5-flow conjecture (stated on the OPG page): for bridgeless cubic G, the three unit vectors of an S²-flow at a vertex sum to zero, hence lie equidistant on a great circle, so composing with the map q gives a nowhere-zero 5-flow; the 5-flow conjecture reduces to bridgeless cubic graphs.

The 5-flow conjecture reduces to bridgeless cubic graphs; composing an S^2-valued flow phi with the antipodal map q: S^2 -> {-4,...,4} of the node's second conjecture yields a nowhere-zero 5-flow. The OPG page notes the two conjectures together imply Tutte's 5-flow conjecture.

A minimal counterexample to CDC is a 3-connected cubic graph G. By Tutte's theorem G has an induced nonseparating circuit C; in cubic G this makes G−E(C) connected (if C is Hamiltonian, G is 3-edge-colorable and has a CDC anyway), so the conjecture applied to S=C yields a CDC of G.

Given a simple digraph D with min out-degree r, colour the underlying edges so that the colour class of vertex v consists of the underlying edges of v's out-arcs (n colours, each class of size >= r). A cycle of length <= ceil(n/r) with no two incident edges of the same colour orients into a directed cycle of D of the same length. The source paper proves exactly this: Conjecture 4 implies Caccetta-Haggkvist.

Given a digraph D with min out-degree r, color each edge of its underlying graph by its tail: n color classes of size >= r. In a cycle of length <= ceil(n/r) with no two incident edges sharing a color, each edge is 'claimed' by one endpoint and no vertex claims two incident cycle edges, so by counting each cycle vertex claims exactly one, making the cycle directed of length <= ceil(n/r). The paper proves this implication explicitly.

Stated explicitly in arXiv:1809.08324: the bipartite short-cycle conjecture (out-degree > n/(k+1) in each part forces girth <= 2k) is implied by the Caccetta-Haggkvist conjecture, via applying CH to an auxiliary digraph built from the bipartite digraph.

Stated in arXiv:1809.08324: the asymmetric bipartite conjecture (k*alpha + beta > 1 forces girth <= 2k) implies Caccetta-Haggkvist by letting beta tend to 0 in a bipartite encoding of a digraph with min out-degree r.

Setting alpha = beta > 1/(k+1) in the asymmetric conjecture (then k*alpha + beta > 1) recovers exactly the symmetric bipartite conjecture with out-degree > n/(k+1) in both parts. The source paper states Conjecture 1.5 is stronger than Conjecture 1.2 as the case alpha = beta.

Set α = β in Conjecture 1.5: out-degree > n/(k+1) in both parts of equal size n means α = β > 1/(k+1), so kα+β > 1, and the conclusion girth ≤ 2k is identical. The paper states Conjecture 1.5 is stronger than Conjecture 1.2 (the α=β case).

Take |A|=|B|=n and alpha=beta=(floor(n/(k+1))+1)/n. Out-degree > n/(k+1) means out-degree >= alpha n = beta n in both parts, and k·alpha+beta = (k+1)(floor(n/(k+1))+1)/n > 1, so the asymmetric conjecture yields girth <= 2k, which is the symmetric bipartite Caccetta-Haggkvist statement.

Setting alpha = beta (slightly above 1/(k+1), so that k alpha + beta > 1) in the asymmetric bipartite Caccetta-Haggkvist conjecture recovers the symmetric out-degree > n/(k+1) version; the paper states Conjecture 1.5 is stronger and includes 1.2 as the alpha=beta case.

With the same constant k: if a k-arc-strong digraph D has two arc-disjoint strongly connected spanning subdigraphs D1, D2, then D1 contains an out-branching rooted at u and D2 an in-branching rooted at v (any strong spanning subdigraph contains branchings from/to every root), and these are arc-disjoint.

The paper states Conjecture 4.4 ({K2-digon, K_k, F} heroic for every oriented forest F) is equivalent to the special case H = TT_k of Conjecture 4.2, since forbidding the edgeless K_k in a digon-free digraph is interchangeable with forbidding TT_k (every tournament on 2^k vertices contains TT_k).

Oriented complete multipartite graphs contain no induced K1 + P-vec2 (an isolated vertex forces its non-neighbours into its own part, contradicting adjacency inside the path), so they form a subclass of {K1+P-vec2}-free digraphs. Hence if Delta(1,2,2) were a hero in {K1+P-vec2}-free digraphs it would be a hero in oriented complete multipartite graphs; the disproof of the latter (arXiv:2202.13306 v2) settles the former negatively.

Oriented complete multipartite digraphs contain no induced K_1 + P->_2 (disjoint union): a vertex nonadjacent to every vertex of the path must share a part with two adjacent path vertices, which lie in different parts. So oriented complete multipartite graphs form a subclass of {K_1+P->_2}-free digraphs, and 'Delta(1,2,2) is a hero' in the larger class restricts to the same statement on the subclass.

A digraph has no induced K_1 + P->_2 (arc plus isolated vertex) iff its underlying graph has no induced K_2 cup K_1, i.e. is complete multipartite. Oriented complete multipartite graphs are thus exactly the digon-free members of the {K_1+P->_2}-free digraphs, so heroism of Delta(1,2,2) in the larger class restricts to the oriented question.

A k-extension adds k vertices one at a time; Conjecture 9 (unvd(D) <= C * unvd(D-v) for acyclic D) applied k times multiplies the unavoidability number by at most C^k, keeping it linear in |V| for each fixed k. The paper states Conjecture 11 'would follow from Conjecture 9'.

Paper-stated conditional implication: Conjecture 9 (unvd(D) <= C*unvd(D-v)) applied to the k added vertices, TOGETHER with Sumner's conjecture (oriented trees of order n are (2n-2)-unavoidable), gives C^k(2n-2)-unavoidability of k-extensions of trees. Not standalone: it additionally needs Sumner's conjecture, which is outside this pair.

Reversing a single arc is a locally finite perturbation, and for tournaments an induced copy of T is a subtournament copy. So Conjecture 24 supplies, for every non-transitive finite tournament H, a countable H-free tournament in which any single arc reversal creates H, answering Problem 23 for all non-transitive H (the transitive cases are handled by known finite examples noted in the paper).

Reversing a single arc is a locally finite perturbation, and for tournaments subtournament containment equals induced containment; so the source's S_T witnesses that every non-transitive T belongs to the class the target asks to characterize (transitive T are excluded in the infinite setting by Ramsey).

Forcing implies Sidorenko (standard, also in the directed setting: the forcing property is defined via the Sidorenko-type inequality with equality only for quasirandom targets). Bipartite oriented B with a homomorphism to K-vec2 either has a cycle in its underlying graph (then Conjecture 1.7 gives forcing, hence Sidorenko) or is a forest, for which the directed Sidorenko property is easy/known.

Problem 2.15 asks for the full complexity classification of circular F-colourability over all fixed F; Conjecture 2.16 is the assertion resolving the cyclic-F half of that dichotomy (NP-completeness whenever F contains a directed cycle; acyclic F are trivially polynomial). Solving the classification problem settles the conjecture.

The question whether every orientation of C4 is Eulerian-avoidable is the instance of the general characterization problem 'which digraphs are Eulerian-avoidable' restricted to the four orientations of the 4-cycle; a full characterization answers it.

An n-vertex tournament is an n-chromatic oriented graph, so g(k) <= f(k) where f is the general oriented-graph function of Problem __00 and g its tournament restriction; the conjecture g(k) <= k^{4/3+o(1)} is the tournament instance of the same extremal question. Determining f resolves the tournament case up to the conjectured exponent.

A digraph H admits constants c_epsilon for every epsilon > 0 (Question __02) exactly when the directed chromatic threshold epsilon_H of Question __03 equals 0. Hence determining epsilon_H for all H resolves which H satisfy __02.

Characterizing the minimal families of tournaments H1,...,Hk with {K-vec2, K-digon2, H1,...,Hk} heroic is the restriction of the general heroic-set characterization Problem 1.2 to sets consisting of the single arc, the digon, and tournaments; the general characterization answers it.

Take m=2 in the multicolour statement: a 2-colouring of E(K_n) encodes a graph G and its complement, 'k vertices coloured according to χ' is an induced copy of the k-vertex graph H encoded by χ, and 'n^ε vertices using at most 1 colour' is a clique or stable set of size n^ε. Quantifying over all 2-colourings χ of E(K_k) recovers exactly the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture.

Take m=2 colours (edge/non-edge of a fixed H on k vertices): the multicolour conjecture then yields either k vertices coloured according to H (an induced copy of H) or n^eps vertices using at most one colour (a clique or independent set). So the classical Erdos-Hajnal conjecture is the m=2 instance.

Take m=2 and colour E(K_k) by edges/non-edges of H: a 2-colouring of E(K_n) is a graph, k vertices coloured per chi form an induced H, and n^eps vertices using at most one colour form a clique or independent set - exactly Erdos-Hajnal for H.

A graph of VC-dimension ≤ d contains no induced copy of the shattering bipartite pattern B_{d+1} (d+1 vertices plus a witness vertex for each subset), since an induced copy would shatter d+1 vertices by neighbourhood traces. So VC-dim ≤ d graphs form a hereditary subclass of B_{d+1}-free graphs, and EH applied to H=B_{d+1} gives the n^{ε(d)} clique/stable set. The source paper itself calls Conjecture 4.1 the VC-dimension specialisation of Erdős–Hajnal.

If χ(G) ≥ c then G contains a subgraph of minimum degree ≥ c−1, hence average degree ≥ c−1; applying Thomassen's conjecture with average degree d(k,g) yields a subgraph of girth > g and average degree ≥ k, so c(k,g)=d(k,g)+1 works. The 1808.01605 paper states its Conjecture 6 is a weakening of Thomassen's conjecture.

If chi(G) >= d+2 then G has a subgraph of minimum (hence average) degree >= d+1 (take a critical subgraph). Choosing d = d(k,g) from Thomassen's conjecture yields a subgraph of average degree >= k and girth > g, exactly the chromatic version with c(k,g)=d+2.

Conjecture 6.1 is the instance of Problem 1.1 with P = P_{C_{2ℓ}} (induced-C_{2ℓ}-free graphs), a hereditary property missing the bipartite graph C_{2ℓ}; a full determination of ex(Γ,P) over (c,t)-sparse Γ decides the conjectured C·t^{1−1/ℓ}n^{1+1/ℓ} bound.

Dense random graphs G(n,p) are whp (c,t)-sparse (edge density between any two linear-size sets is ≤ 1−c), and 2405.05902 explicitly introduces Problem 1.1 as the deterministic generalization of this Alon–Krivelevich–Samotij random-graph question; determining ex(Γ,P) for all (c,t)-sparse Γ and bipartite-missing hereditary P gives the precise order of ex(G(n,p),P).
By definition m(n,k) = min over n-vertex graphs G of e(G) − u(G,k), so a full answer to Question 2.1 (determine u(G,k) for every G) determines the exact value of m(n,k) by minimizing over G.

Standard fractional-covering bound: |V(G)|/a(G) <= va_f(G), where a(G) is the maximum size of an induced forest. So va_f(G) <= 2 for planar G forces an induced forest on >= n/2 vertices, which is exactly the Albertson-Berman conjecture. The paper's own context states this implication.

If va_f(G) <= 2, an optimal fractional cover by induced forests has total weight <= 2 while covering all n vertices, so n <= sum_F w_F|F| <= 2 max_F |F|, giving an induced forest on >= n/2 vertices. This is the Albertson-Berman conjecture; the paper states the implication (|V|/a(G) <= va_f(G)).

If the graphs critical for 5-choosability on the torus are exactly the 6-critical ones, then a toroidal G fails 5-choosability iff it contains a 6-critical subgraph iff chi(G)>=6, i.e. iff G is not 5-colorable; conversely 5-colorability always follows from 5-choosability, and the paper states Conjectures 2 and 3 are equivalent (via Thomassen's classification of 6-critical toroidal graphs).

Thomassen's classification shows the 6-critical toroidal graphs (K6, C3+C5, K2+H7, T11) cannot occur in a torus drawing of edge-width >= 4, so such graphs are 5-colorable; under Conjecture 3 (5-choosable iff 5-colorable) they are then 5-choosable. The paper presents Conjecture 4 as an intermediate step towards Conjecture 3.

Apply E[F^-] <= E[F] to G = K_n and combine with the paper's theorem that the expected face count of a uniformly random orientable embedding of K_n is ln(n)+O(1); this yields the conjectured ln(n)+O(1) bound for non-orientable random embeddings of K_n.

The same paper establishes that the orientable random embedding of K_n has expected face count ln(n) + O(1); combining this with the general comparison E[F⁻] <= E[F] (Conjecture 9.6) applied to G = K_n gives the non-orientable bound E[F⁻(K_n)] <= ln(n) + O(1), i.e. Conjecture 9.5.

Parameter monotonicity: the conjectured bound E[F] <= n/3 + 1 for every simple n-vertex graph is a concrete linear bound, hence immediately gives E[F] = O(n) for uniformly random orientable embeddings.

Both concern the expected number of faces E[F] of a uniformly random orientable embedding of an arbitrary n-vertex simple graph; the explicit bound E[F] <= n/3 + 1 is O(n), so Conjecture 4 of 2202.07746 immediately yields Conjecture 1 of 2103.05036 (which that later paper in fact proved with constant π²/6).
Both concern the expected number of faces of a uniformly random orientable embedding of an arbitrary simple n-vertex graph; the quantitative bound E[F] <= n/3 + 1 immediately gives E[F] = O(n).
The bound E[F] <= n/3 + 1 for every simple n-vertex graph is in particular O(n), the target's statement for uniformly random orientable embeddings.

Planar graphs have layered treewidth at most 3 (Dujmovic-Morin-Wood), so if every class of bounded layered treewidth has bounded queue-number, planar graphs have constant queue number. (Both statements are now resolved; the implication was the known route.)
Planar graphs have layered treewidth at most 3 (Dujmovic-Morin-Wood), so if graphs of bounded layered treewidth have bounded queue-number, then planar graphs have constant queue-number.

An n^{2-o(1)} lower bound (no O(n^{2-eps}) algorithm for any eps>0) for map isomorphism is in particular a truly superlinear omega(n polylog n) lower bound for map isomorphism, which is what the subproblem asks to establish (conditionally).

If no O(n^{2-eps}) algorithm exists for map isomorphism for any eps > 0, then in particular no O(n polylog n) algorithm exists (n polylog n = O(n^{1.5})), which is an (even unconditional) truly-superlinear lower bound as sought in 2008.01616__01.

Setting t=0 gives M_{n,0}=K_n and the conjectured formula reads cr(K_n)=H(n), the Harary-Hill value (1/4)*floor(n/2)*floor((n-1)/2)*floor((n-2)/2)*floor((n-3)/2). So the Harary-Hill conjecture is the t=0 instance of the K_n-minus-t-matching conjecture (the paper is explicitly a generalization of Hill's conjecture); if the paper requires t>=1, it is the boundary case of the common generalization.

Outerplanar graphs are planar, and their cop number is at most 2 (Theorem 3 of the same paper), so classifying planar graphs by cop number i in {1,2,3} restricted to the subclass of outerplanar graphs is exactly the 1-cop-win vs 2-cop-win dichotomy asked in __01.

MWIS with unit weights is MIS, so a combinatorial polynomial-time algorithm for Maximum Weight Independent Set in perfect graphs is in particular a combinatorial polynomial-time algorithm for MIS in perfect graphs.
A combinatorial poly-time algorithm for Maximum Weight Independent Set on perfect graphs solves the unweighted MIS case by setting all weights to 1; both are the Grotschel-Lovasz-Schrijver problem.

A polynomial-time algorithm for Maximum Weight Independent Set on even-hole-free graphs solves the unweighted maximum independent set problem on even-hole-free graphs (unit weights), settling the open complexity question in 1912.11246__01.

(even hole, K4)-free graphs form a subclass of even-hole-free graphs, so resolving MIS on even-hole-free graphs (positively) settles the (even hole, K4)-free half of 2001.01607__03; the (theta, triangle)-free half is separate (thetas contain even holes, but triangle-freeness is an extra restriction).

The conjectured dichotomy places every spider S_{i,j,k} on the polynomial side, so it would determine (as P) the complexity of MIS on S_{i,j,k}-free graphs for the cases containing P7, S_{1,1,3}, S_{1,2,2} asked in 2001.01607__04.

O_k-free graphs have induced cycle packing number < k, hence induced odd cycle packing number iocp < k (odd cycles are cycles). So tractability of MIS on bounded-iocp graphs implies polynomial MIS on O_k-free graphs for each fixed k.

The bounded sub-determinant IP conjecture explicitly yields (its 'in particular' clause) polynomial stable set for all graphs with ocp(G) <= k; restricting to graphs embedded in a surface of arbitrary Euler genus gives 1908.06300__01 by hypothesis-class containment.
The source explicitly asserts stable set is polynomial for every fixed ocp(G) <= k on all graphs, which contains the subclass of graphs embedded in a surface of arbitrary Euler genus.

Any family of vertex-disjoint pairwise-anticomplete induced odd cycles is a family of disjoint odd cycles, so iocp(G) <= ocp(G); graphs with ocp <= k (embedded in any surface) thus have iocp <= k. Tractability of MIS on bounded-iocp graphs (2206.00594__02) therefore covers the class in 1908.06300__01.

Weighted Min Vertex Cover is a monotone FO minimization problem; a local-search PTAS for all monotone FO optimization problems on hereditary classes with (strongly) sublinear separators would give the weighted-MVC PTAS asked for in 2105.01780__00, whose 'more general' setting is exactly hereditary classes with sublinear separators.

The open 5-Coloring cases for H-free graphs with H = P4 plus an induced subgraph of rP3 are instances (k = 5, specific linear forests H) of the general k-Coloring dichotomy classification problem for H-free graphs.

(K3, S_{1,2,3}) is one of the five remaining unresolved pairs in the boundedness-of-clique-width classification of (H1,H2)-free graphs, so deciding all five pairs answers whether (triangle, S_{1,2,3})-free graphs have bounded cliquewidth.

A semi-induced half-graph H_{2t,2t} contains K_{t,t} as a subgraph (take the top half of one side against the bottom half of the other), so K_{t,t}-subgraph-free graphs are H_{2t,2t}-free; FPT Grundy Coloring on H_{t,t}-free graphs for all t therefore covers the K_{t,t}-free case.

The per-class question (does a given class G admit a constant bounding gamma/rho) is an instance of the full characterization problem of all classes with uniformly bounded domination-to-packing ratio; the characterization answers each instance.

(1,r)-cover-free families with t = O(r^2 log|F|/log r) yield deterministic non-adaptive reconstruction of max-degree-Delta graphs with O(Delta^2 log n / log Delta) queries (the paper's CFF-to-reconstruction reduction), which is o(Delta^3 log(n/Delta)); non-adaptive algorithms are a special case of adaptive ones.

Replacing each edge of a graph G embedded in Sigma by a digon gives a digraph whose dichromatic number equals chi(G); hence Sigma-4-Dicolourability restricted to bidirected inputs is 4-colorability on Sigma, and a polynomial algorithm for the k=4 dicolouring problem would solve 1010.2472__00. Requires the dicolouring problem to admit digons.

Induction on ν: for an r-partite r-uniform H, Conjecture 4.3 gives k(r−1) vertices whose deletion drops the matching number by ≥k; by induction the remainder has a cover of size (r−1)(ν−k), so adding the deleted vertices yields a cover of size ≤ (r−1)ν, i.e. τ ≤ (r−1)ν. The authors explicitly propose it as a weakening of Lovász's conjecture that still implies Ryser's conjecture.

Iterate: each round deletes k_i(r-1) vertices lowering nu by >= k_i, and the hypergraph stays r-partite r-uniform. When nu reaches 0 every edge meets the deleted set, a cover of size <= (r-1) * sum k_i <= (r-1)nu, i.e. tau <= (r-1)nu. The paper states it is a weakening of Lovasz's conjecture that still implies Ryser.

Conjecture 6.2 asserts the Turán exponent of a k-partite k-uniform H is controlled as k−Θ(1/d_max(H)); for the 3-partite Latin-square hypergraph H_L one has d_max(H_L)=Θ(d), so 6.2 yields ex(n,H_L)=n^{3−Θ(1/d)}, which is Conjecture 6.4. The paper states 6.4's prediction matches d_max(H_L)=Θ(d) 'via Conjecture 6.2'. (6.2's statement is truncated in the record, hence medium confidence.)

If the extremal symmetric intersecting A ⊂ [k]^n are set-intersecting, they are generated by a symmetric intersecting set family B ⊂ P([n]); the orbit-averaging bound Σ_γ|B∩γB| = |B|²|Γ|/n forces every B∈B to have |B| ≥ √n, which plausibly caps |A| at k^{n−cn^{1/2}}, giving the polynomial gain with δ=1/2. The final counting step (bounding over all generators B) is not verified.

A 57-regular Moore graph of diameter 2 and girth 5 is a (3250,57,0,1) strongly regular graph; girth 5 forces lambda=0, so it is triangle-free and distinct from the seven known triangle-free SRGs (C5, Petersen, Clebsch, Hoffman-Singleton, Gewirtz, the (77,16,0,4) graph, Higman-Sims). Its existence would therefore provide an eighth triangle-free strongly regular graph. The OPG page for the target states this implication explicitly.

The paper proves that non-semisimple finite rings R give non-prime X_R, and that for semisimple R = prod F_{q_i} the Cayley graph satisfies X_R ≅ prod K_{q_i} (tensor product of complete graphs). Hence the open content of 'when is X_R prime?' (Q4.28) is exactly the primeness question for tensor products of complete graphs restricted to prime-power orders, i.e. a special case of Q4.31, which asks it for arbitrary positive integers n_i.

Intersecting winning families are among the balanced monotone families considered, so p_monotone(t) >= p_intersecting(t); hence p_monotone(t) -> 0 forces p_intersecting(t) -> 0. The paper states the chain p_monotone >= p_intersecting >= p_dict and calls Conjecture 2.2 'progressively stronger' than 2.1.

By the identity p_intersecting(t,n) = fractional-independence ᾱ(K(n)^{□t}) (K(n) the Kneser graph on {0,1}^n, □ the Hamming product), Conjecture 2.6 is an exact graph-theoretic restatement of Conjecture 2.1: the double limit tending to 0 is the same statement as p_intersecting(t) -> 0.

ε*(α) > 0 gives a uniform gap ᾱ(G) - α*(G) over all G with ᾱ(G) >= α; applied along the Hamming powers K(n)^{□t} this drives ᾱ(K(n)^{□t}) down at each power, forcing the double limit to 0. The paper states explicitly that Conjecture 2.8 would imply Conjecture 2.6 (and hence Levine's conjecture).

Conjecture 2.9 (ε** > 0) is exactly Conjecture 2.8 (ε* > 0) restricted to the case where the positively-correlated random-subset distribution with Bernoulli(1/2) marginals is the plain binomial distribution (vertices included independently with probability 1/2), as stated in the paper; so ε* > 0 for the general class yields ε** > 0.

The paper states that Conjecture 9 (f(K_m,p) = 2^{o(m)} p^{-2m/3+c_m} in the Subgraph Query Game) together with the proven Theorem 10 implies both parts of Conjecture 7: specializing the query bound at the appropriate p gives the diagonal rate 2^{(2/3+o(1))n} and the off-diagonal rate n^{(2/3+o(1))m} for the online random Ramsey numbers r̃_rand.

Since ln(pn²) <= 2 ln n for all p <= 1, the asymptotic E[F] = (1+o(1)) ln(pn²) for random embeddings of G(n,p) gives E[F] = O(log n) for every edge-probability function p(n). Caveat: the target asserts the bound for almost all graphs (E over embedding only), so the implication is clean under the a.a.s.-per-graph reading of the source.

λ(d,1) = (1+o(1))/e is the s = 1 instance of the problem of obtaining tight asymptotic bounds for λ(d,s) over essentially all admissible (d,s); resolving the general problem determines the asymptotics at s = 1, matching the conjectured lower bound (1-2^{-d})^{2^d - 1} -> 1/e.

The conjecture λ(d,1)=(1+o(1))/e is the s=1 instance of the general open problem of obtaining tight asymptotic bounds for λ(d,s) over essentially all admissible (d,s): a tight determination for all admissible parameters would in particular decide whether the proven lower bound (1−2^{-d})^{2^d−1} → 1/e is asymptotically sharp at s=1.

The target posits, for every radius r, a second phase transition threshold t(n) for r-neighbourhood shotgun reconstructibility of G(n,p); the source asks to determine that sharp threshold for the two unresolved radii r ∈ {1,2}, i.e. it is the r <= 2 instance of the general threshold statement.

The paper states (context of Conjecture 3.1) that the disproportionate bipartition statement for measures on S^1 would imply, by a simple inductive argument splitting [n]=P∪Q and recursing on each interval, that f(n) ≤ 2n−2; the matching lower bound f(n) ≥ 2n−2 is already proved via Segal-Halevi's construction. Hence Conjecture 3.1 implies f(n)=2n−2.

The paper states explicitly that Conjecture 4 (vec-t(n)=Θ(√(n/log n))) follows from Conjecture 3 (vec-a(n)=Θ(√(n log n))): the inequality vec-t(n) ≥ n/vec-a(n) turns the conjectured upper bound O(√(n log n)) on the acyclic number into the missing lower bound Ω(√(n/log n)) on the dichromatic number, while the upper bound vec-t(n) ≤ (√2+o(1))√(n/log n) is already proved.

U_t(n) is the minimum number of lazy transpositions in a t-uniformity network on n positions (shuffling t distinguishable counters), and the companion papers are by the same authors. Setting t=2 in the conjectured formula U_t(n)=tn−C(t+1,2) gives exactly 2n−3, which is the statement of Conjecture 1 in 2208.06630. So the 2-uniformity conjecture is the t=2 instance of the general problem.

If every finite family F containing a forest is k-nice for all k ≥ k0(F) (Question 1.1), then in particular it is k-nice for infinitely many k. The paper itself poses the conjecture as 'a weaker version of Question 1.1'.
If F is k-nice for all k >= k0(F), then it is k-nice for infinitely many k; the paper poses the target as the weaker version of the source question.

Graphs embeddable in a fixed surface of genus g form a proper minor-closed family (genus is minor-monotone and some graph has larger genus). So the linear bound xc(P_sp.trees(G))=O(|V|) for all proper minor-closed families restricts to the bounded-genus conjecture; the paper introduces Conjecture 2 as the generalization of Conjecture 1.

Graphs embeddable in a fixed surface form a proper minor-closed family, so the O(|V|) spanning-tree-polytope extension-complexity conjecture for minor-closed families contains the fixed-surface version as a special case.

The conjecture that the induced arithmetic removal lemma (Theorem 1.14) holds for arbitrary Z-coefficient patterns over arbitrary abelian groups is precisely the proposed resolution of the open problem of extending the lemma beyond complexity-1 patterns over F_q to higher complexity and general abelian groups (including Z); its truth settles both extensions asked for.

Problem 1.10 (is f(d)/f_{≤2}(d) subexponential in n=2^{d-1}?) is exactly part (iii) of Problem 1.2, which asks for the order of magnitude of the four ratios and which of them is exponential in n; the paper's own context says Problem 1.10 'addresses Problem 1.2 (iii)'. Determining the order of magnitude of ratio (iii) answers the subexponentiality question.

The lamination conjecture together with the already-proved lower bound n(2,d) > (1−o(1))d²/2 yields lim n(2,d)/d² = 1/2 (as stated in the record); in particular the limit exists, answering the open question affirmatively.

If T(G) = Θ̃(√|G|) uniformly over all finite groups G, then T(p) = Θ̃(√p) for primes p (far below the current O(p^{3/4+ε}) upper bound, which relies on subgroups), and T(G) depends on the structure of G beyond its order only up to polylogarithmic factors — settling both parts of the question.

A closed Riemannian surface with cut locus (hence systole) bounded below by 1 and area at most α has genus bounded in terms of α by the systolic inequality for surfaces (area ≥ c·g/log²g when sys ≥ 1). So if the cop number of Riemannian surfaces is bounded by a function of the genus (positive answer to the first question), the supremum over the class in the second question is finite.

If every forest H gives a polynomially chi-bounded class of H-free graphs, then in particular Forb(H) is chi-bounded for every forest, which is the Gyarfas-Sumner conjecture; the 'only if' direction of the target is a known theorem (Erdos girth construction), and the paper states its Conjecture 2 is equivalent to Gyarfas-Sumner.

If H-free graphs satisfy chi <= poly(omega) for every forest H, then for K_d(t)-subgraph-free graphs omega < dt, so chi <= poly(dt), polynomial in t for fixed d — exactly multibounding. The 2303.11766 paper states that any forest satisfying the polynomial chi-boundedness conjecture is multibounding.
